description: CIBMTR offers investigators opportunities that extend beyond traditional Working Committee participation. This session will highlight practical ways to leverage CIBMTR resources, mentorship, data, biospecimens, and collaborative networks to advance research and foster career development. Through four investigator perspectives, attendees will learn how engagement with CIBMTR can help build collaborations and professional networks; support mentored research and career development awards; leverage NMDP Biorepository samples to translate laboratory discoveries from the bench back to the bedside and impact clinical practice; and use publicly available CIBMTR datasets to support graduate education and scholarly work. Speakers will share examples of their research, while highlighting their career paths and practical lessons learned through experiences with the Page Scholar Program, mentored K award research, NMDP Biorepository resources, and publicly available CIBMTR datasets. The session will conclude with an interactive panel discussion focused on how investigators at different career stages can identify and pursue CIBMTR opportunities to develop mentorship, collaborations, research projects, and pathways toward research independence.

title: Concurrent: Chronic GVHD, Tissue Regeneration and Fibrosis
keywords: Translational Science; Mechanisms/Pathogenesis; Basic Science; Autoimmune; GVHD
description: Chronic graft versus host disease is associated with substantial morbidity, negatively affecting patients' quality of life and overall outcomes after allogeneic HSCT. Underlying pathophysiology is complex and multipronged and can differ between chronic GVHD target organs. Prolonged dysregulated inflammation leading to fibrotic / sclerotic changes has been identified as one major hallmark. One common manifestation of excessive fibrosis is seen in the skin, leading to sclerodermatous skin chronic GVHD. Another critical target organ is the lung, characterized by bronchiolitis obliterans, a progressively worsening form or airflow obstruction. Historically, treatment options of chronic GVHD beyond steroid first line therapy have been limited, however, with the approval of the BTK/ITK inhibitor ibrutinib, the JAK/STAT inhibitor ruxolitinib, the Rho-associated coiled -coil kinase 2 inhibitor belumosudil and most recently the CSF1R-blocking antibody axatilimab patient outcomes have improved. In this session, Dr. Gerhard Hildebrandt will review novel aspects and targets in the pathophysiology of sclerodermatous chronic GVHD. Dr. Parvathi Ranganathan will focus on current and novel therapeutic targets in the pathophysiology and management of bronchiolitis obliterans. Dr. Daniel Wolff will provide a comprehensive review on how to diagnose and manage chronic GVHD.

title: Plenary: Architects of the Genome: Gene Therapy and Gene Editing
presenters: Mark Osborn; Claire Booth, MBBS, Ph.D.; Harry L Malech, MD
keywords: Gene Therapy; Infection/Infectious Disease; Translational Science; Translational Science; Adoptive Cell Therapy; Basic Science; Adoptive Cell Therapy; Gene Editing; Basic Science; Gene Editing
description: This session will highlight the advances that are at the forefront of how inherited and acquired diseases are and can be treated through genetic intervention. Featuring talks by Dr. Claire Booth and Dr. Harry Malech, the symposium will explore complementary approaches spanning clinical gene therapy and next-generation genome editing. Dr. Booth will discuss the translation of gene therapy highlighting the challenges and opportunities of delivering durable therapeutic benefit. Dr. Malech will detail the first in clinic prime editing strategy, a versatile genome-editing technology capable of making precise genetic changes without requiring double-strand DNA breaks. Together, these presentations will showcase how advances in vector engineering, genome editing, and cellular therapy are converging to create increasingly precise, personalized, and generalized medicines. The session will provide a historical and forward-looking perspective on the evolving architecture of genetic medicine—and how today's innovations are shaping the next generation of therapies.

title: Concurrent: AI at the Bedside: From Signals to Decisions to Partnership
description:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly moving from the background of clinical research into the front lines of patient care. This session will bring together three complementary perspectives on how AI is reshaping healthcare. 
Erin Craig will discuss AI-enabled patient monitoring and how longitudinal physiologic data may help detect clinically meaningful changes earlier and more continuously. Mirco Friedrich will explore emerging AI agents and their potential to synthesize complex clinical information, integrate prior knowledge, and support clinical reasoning and decision-making. Hugo Campos will examine AI from the patient perspective, focusing on patient agency, access to information, trust, and how these technologies may change the relationship between patients and clinicians. 
Together, the speakers will examine how AI could change not only what we can detect and predict, but also how decisions are made and how patients participate in their care.

title: Concurrent: Evolution of Donor Selection, Using Biology and Technology to Enhance Post-HCT Outcomes [NMDP]
keywords: Myeloid Malignancies; Clinical Science; Graft-Versus-Tumor; Graft-Versus-Host Disease
description: This session examines how contemporary donor selection strategies are reshaping outcomes in hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT), integrating biological insight with emerging technologies to refine donor-recipient matching. The first presentation addresses the impact of donor age on post-HCT outcomes, reviewing evidence on how donor age influences graft function, relapse risk, transplant-related mortality, and long-term survival, and discussing how age should be weighed alongside other donor selection criteria in clinical decision-making. The second presentation explores the modernization of stem cell donor selection through artificial intelligence, highlighting how AI-driven algorithms and predictive modeling are being applied to donor registry searches, matching optimization, and outcome prediction—offering clinicians new tools to identify optimal donors more efficiently and accurately than traditional selection methods. The third presentation focuses on donor HLA typing strategies designed to enhance graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) effects, examining how refined HLA matching and mismatch strategies can strengthen the immunologic benefits of allogeneic HCT while managing the balance between GVL activity and graft-versus-host disease risk. Together, these presentations offer a comprehensive view of how biological understanding and technological innovation are converging to advance donor selection practices, with direct implications for improving survival and quality of life in HCT recipients. Attendees will gain updated, evidence-based perspectives applicable to clinical practice and translational research.

description: As CAR T-cell therapies and bispecific antibodies continue to transform the treatment landscape for lymphoma and multiple myeloma, clinicians face increasingly complex decisions regarding treatment selection and sequencing. This session will explore the biological and clinical factors that influence whether and when to use CAR T-cell therapy, bispecific antibodies, and transplantation. The session will include examination of the biological rationale for sequencing CAR-T versus bispecific therapy, as well as a review of current evidence and emerging data on sequencing outcomes in lymphoma and multiple myeloma. Through case-based discussions, faculty will apply these principles to real-world treatment decisions, including the evolving role of transplantation within contemporary treatment pathways. By integrating biology, clinical scenarios, and emerging evidence, this session will provide attendees with a practical framework to help inform individualized treatment strategies and optimize therapy and for patients with lymphoma and multiple myeloma.

title: Plenary: The New Frontier of Tolerance: GVHD in the PTCy Era
keywords: GVHD; Clinical Practice; Translational Science; Basic Science; Mechanisms/Pathogenesis
description: Post-transplantation cyclophosphamide (PTCy) has had a major impact on the field of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation by decreasing severe graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), even when using donors that are not fully HLA-matched. This has improved GVHD outcomes and also access to transplant, particularly for individuals of racial/ethnic minorities. Multiple randomized phase III studies now have established PTCy as a standard-of-care also in the HLA-matched donor setting. This session explores the mechanistic biology underlying GVHD prevention by PTCy, ongoing efforts in clinical optimization including PTCy dose optimization and which adjunct immunosuppressive agent(s) to pair with PTCy, and how to pick the best donor in the PTCy era.

description: In this session we are going to review the rapidly expanding field of cellular immunotherapy for the treatment of autoimmune diseases. Dr. Dimitrios Mougiakakos from the University Magdeburg will review what we know about the mechanism by which CAR T-cells reset the immune system and reestablish immune tolerance to self antigens. Dr. Saira Sheikh from the University of North Carolina will review the early experience with cellular immunotherapy in rheumatologic diseases such as lupus nephritis. Last, Dr. Claudio Brunstein from the Cleveland Clinic will review care collaborative models of patient selection and clinical integration between rheumatologists and cellular therapy specialists.

ep_category: Translational Science, Graft-Versus-Tumor, Myeloid Malignancies, Clinical Practice
title: Concurrent: The Relapse Challenge: Novel Maintenance, MRD Tracking, and Interventions for Post-Therapy Relapse
keywords: Translational Science; Graft-Versus-Tumor; Myeloid Malignancies; Clinical Practice
description: Disease relapse remains the greatest obstacle to long-term success for patients with AML undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT). Despite decades of progress in reducing early transplant-related mortality and severe GVHD, the incidence of relapse has changed remarkably little. Two parallel advances now offer a path forward. First, increasingly sensitive assays for measurable residual disease (MRD) allow far more precise risk stratification before and after HCT, though how best to incorporate MRD into eligibility criteria, stratification, and trial endpoints remains unclear. Second, the growing armamentarium of targeted agents in AML has made post-HCT maintenance therapy feasible and has raised the possibility that these drugs act not only on leukemia but also augment graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) activity. This session brings these threads together. We will first review the preclinical evidence that inhibition of specific pathways after HCT can cultivate effective GVL, reframing maintenance as an immunologic as well as a cytotoxic intervention. We will then examine the current landscape of MRD assays in AML around the time of HCT, and how future trial design should be built around them. Finally, we will review the current state of practice for maintenance therapy after HCT for AML. Underlying all three talks is an uncomfortable reality: post-HCT maintenance has become widespread practice in the absence of a definitively positive randomized phase 3 trial. This session will examine how the biology, the biomarkers, and the evidence can be brought into alignment.

increasingly individualized transplant approaches may further improve outcomes
and expand the path toward cure.

title: Plenary: Beyond the Cytokine Storm: Navigating Toxicities Across Evolving Cellular Therapy Platforms
keywords: Adoptive Cell Therapy; Plasma Cell Disorders; Translational Science; CAR-T; Lymphoid Malignancies; Clinical Practice; Mechanisms/Pathogenesis
description: Acute clinical management of cytokine toxicities such as CRS and ICANS are well established for cellular therapies. However, non-canonical toxicities such as cytopenias (termed ICAHT), non-ICANS neurologic toxicities (NINTs), and immune effector cell-associated enterocolitis (IEC-EC), while less common, are important causes of morbidity and mortality. In addition, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, approved as a standard-of-care therapy for metastatic melanoma, is associated with unique toxicities and requirements different from CRS and ICANS. In this session, recent mechanistic data and clinical management approaches to toxicities other than CRS and ICANS will be detailed for approved cellular therapies in B cell malignancies, multiple myeloma, and melanoma.
